title: Jupiter: The Failed Star with a 300-Mile-High Volcano
summary:
You're not even close to leaving the solar system when you pull into orbit around Jupiter, but you'd swear you've just entered a new one. Your ship's scanners flash with readings of nearby worlds and faint rings. Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system, rules a system of its own. Some astronomers even call it a failed star. Welcome to the realm of giants.

Jupiter is a gas giant — a ball of mostly hydrogen and helium large enough to hold more than 1,300 Earths. There's no solid surface to explore. If you tried to skydive from your ship's airlock, you'd sink deeper into clouds of ammonia and water vapor until the intense pressure and heat compressed the hydrogen around you into a molten liquid. Science fiction writers have proposed exploring Jupiter in hot-air balloons high above the crushing depths, but it's safer to watch its spectacular cloud bands whiz by at more than 300 miles an hour from orbit.

Jupiter sits about 460 million to 507 million miles from the sun, and the trip from Earth takes roughly 13 months. Gravity here is brutal too: weigh 100 pounds on Earth and you'd weigh 253 pounds on Jupiter.

Several of Jupiter's nearly 70 moons grab your attention. Ganymede, the largest moon, is bigger than Mercury and has its own magnetic field. Io is the most volcanic body in the solar system, with volcanoes that spew clouds of yellow sulfur 300 miles high. And Europa, a frozen moon, might hide a liquid ocean beneath its icy crust. Scientists believe that ocean could even contain life.

Jupiter also has the Great Red Spot, a hurricane that has raged for centuries. Nearly three Earths could span it. And despite being the largest planet, Jupiter has the shortest day — just 10 hours — because it spins so fast.

But be careful: Jupiter generates radiation levels more than a thousand times the lethal dose. Set shields at maximum!
why_it_matters: Gas giants like Jupiter are natural laboratories for how solar systems form, and its icy moon Europa is now one of the best places to search for life beyond Earth — so the questions this planet raises reach far past a single world and shape what space agencies build next.

background_read: Jupiter is so large that all the other planets in the solar system could fit inside it with room to spare, and it is roughly eleven times wider than Earth. It is made mostly of hydrogen and helium — the same two elements that make up the Sun — which is why some astronomers nicknamed it a 'failed star'. A real star needs to be many times more massive than Jupiter before nuclear fusion can ignite in its core; Jupiter came close, but never lit up.

NASA's Juno spacecraft has been orbiting Jupiter, measuring its gravity, magnetic field and swirling atmosphere, while earlier probes dropped directly into its clouds. Jupiter's magnetic field is vastly stronger than Earth's and traps charged particles into radiation belts intense enough to damage electronics, which is why spacecraft cannot linger close to the planet.

Its moons are worlds in their own right. Ganymede (Jupiter's largest moon, and the biggest moon in the solar system) is larger than the planet Mercury. Io is squeezed and heated by Jupiter's enormous gravity, and that is what keeps its volcanoes erupting. Europa's cracked ice shell may cover a salty ocean, and NASA is sending a spacecraft to study that ice and look for signs the ocean could support life.

perspectives.description: Jupiter is effectively a solar system in miniature, with dozens of moons, its own faint rings and a storm bigger than Earth. Missions like Juno keep revealing new detail, and Europa's possible ocean makes it a top target in the search for life.

perspectives.perspective: Critics of the framing and the spending
perspectives.description: Calling Jupiter a 'failed star' is catchy but misleading, since it never had a real chance of igniting and is simply a planet. Others ask whether the money poured into distant moons would be better spent solving problems on Earth.
Jupiter's huge gravity shaped the whole solar system, steering comets and asteroids, and comparing it with Earth helps scientists work out what makes a planet habitable in the first place.

Future missions to Europa and Io should reveal whether a hidden ocean really exists and how Io's volcanoes work, while studying Jupiter's atmosphere may explain how giant planets form around other stars.
